subject: Pathology
summary: Chronic bronchitis is a form of COPD defined by a productive cough for ≥3 months in ≥2 consecutive years, caused by long‑term airway irritation. Mucous‑gland hypertrophy and goblet‑cell hyperplasia narrow airways and produce excess mucus.

sections.p: A clinical diagnosis of chronic bronchitis requires a productive cough on most days for at least three months in two consecutive years, after excluding asthma, infection, and heart failure.
b: Reid index >0.5 on histology confirms mucous‑gland hypertrophy
Post‑bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 indicates COPD

t.b: Does the patient have airflow obstruction? A reduced FEV1/FVC (<0.70) confirms COPD, supporting chronic bronchitis.
Are there alternative diagnoses (e.g., pneumonia, heart failure)? Look for increased bronchovascular markings; a normal film does not rule out disease.
Is a bacterial infection driving the current flare? Growth of typical pathogens (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae) guides antibiotic use.

sections.p: Severity is staged by GOLD grades using post‑bronchodilator FEV1 % predicted, and by symptom burden (mMRC dyspnoea scale or CAT score).
b: GOLD 1: FEV1 ≥80% (mild)
GOLD 2: 50–79% (moderate)
GOLD 3: 30–49% (severe)
GOLD 4: <30% (very severe)

sections.p: Chronic irritation of the bronchial epithelium drives glandular hyperplasia and mucus over‑production.
b: Cigarette smoke (most common worldwide)
Biomass fuel smoke (wood, charcoal – major in low‑resource settings)
Occupational dusts/fumes (grain, cotton, silica)
Ambient air pollution (SO₂, NO₂)
Recurrent lower‑respiratory infections (including TB in endemic areas)

sections.p: Patients report a daily productive cough, especially in the morning, with sputum that may become purulent during exacerbations. Over time dyspnoea, wheeze, and cyanosis develop.
b: Coarse crackles and rhonchi on auscultation
Peripheral oedema and jugular venous distension in advanced disease (cor pulmonale)
‘Blue bloater’ phenotype: overweight, cyanosed, CO₂ retention

sections.p: Tests confirm airflow limitation, assess severity, and identify treatable triggers.

t.b: Is there hypoxaemia or hypercapnia? Low PaO₂ or high PaCO₂ signals need for supplemental O₂ or ventilation support.
Is polycythaemia present? Elevated haematocrit reflects chronic hypoxia and may guide oxygen therapy.
Can peak expiratory flow (PEF) be measured? A reduced PEF suggests obstruction, though less precise than spirometry.

sections.p: Complications arise from chronic hypoxia, inflammation, and frequent infections.
b: Acute exacerbation with fever, increased sputum purulence, or rapid dyspnoea
Cor pulmonale (right‑heart failure)
Respiratory failure requiring ventilation
Pulmonary hypertension

sections.p: Treat the irritant exposure, control inflammation, and prevent or treat exacerbations.
b: Smoking cessation (counselling, nicotine replacement, varenicline) – stops disease progression
Vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal) – reduces infection‑driven exacerbations
Long‑acting bronchodilators (LABA or LAMA) – improve airflow and symptoms
Inhaled corticosteroids for frequent exacerbators – lower inflammation, avoid in mild disease due to pneumonia risk
Pulmonary rehabilitation – enhances exercise tolerance
O₂ therapy for PaO₂ <55 mmHg or SaO₂ <88% – prevents cor pulmonale

sections.p: Regular review monitors lung function, symptom control, and comorbidities.
b: Spirometry every 12 months (or sooner after exacerbation)
Assess smoking status and reinforce cessation
Screen for depression and anxiety, common in chronic disease
Educate on early recognition of exacerbation signs

sections.p: Conditions sharing cough and dyspnoea can mislead diagnosis.
b: Asthma – reversible obstruction, often younger onset, eosinophilia
Bronchiectasis – localized dilated bronchi, frequent purulent sputum, CT changes
Heart failure – orthopnoea, peripheral oedema, cardiomegaly on X‑ray

sections.p: Certain findings may appear normal despite disease.
b: Normal chest X‑ray early in disease – does not exclude chronic bronchitis
Spirometry may be within normal limits during a symptom‑free period; repeat if suspicion persists
Sputum culture can be negative in viral‑driven exacerbations

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of breathlessness or chest tightness
New fever, chills, or purulent sputum
Swelling of ankles or sudden weight gain

faq.q: Why does chronic bronchitis cause cyanosis?
faq.a: Mucus plugging and airway narrowing impair gas exchange, leading to low oxygen (hypoxaemia) that makes the skin appear bluish.

faq.q: Can a non‑smoker develop chronic bronchitis?
faq.a: Yes; prolonged exposure to biomass fuel smoke, occupational dusts, or severe air pollution can cause the same airway changes.
Airflow limitation is largely irreversible, but quitting irritants and using bronchodilators can improve symptoms and slow progression.

exam: State the clinical definition of chronic bronchitis and the histologic Reid index threshold.
Explain how you would stage disease severity using GOLD criteria.
List the three most common causes of chronic bronchitis in low‑resource settings and a key management step for each.
